clue.text: Three men in line, each wanting last dance

indicators.note: to want is to lack, so every item lacks its final letter

parts.note: a man is a chap, taken three times

explanation.surface: Three men stand in a queue, each hoping for the final dance of the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: Each CHAP drops its P, leaving CHA three times over, set in a line to spell CHA-CHA-CHA.
explanation.definitionFit: The cha-cha-cha is a Latin ballroom routine originating in Cuba.

clue.text: Hard to be expelled from immaculate social group

indicators.note: something expelled is thrown out, so that letter is removed from the word

parts.note: immaculate means pure, spotless
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A tough character is thrown out of a squeaky-clean clique.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the H out of CHASTE to leave CASTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A caste is a hereditary class in a rigid hierarchy, most famously in India.

clue.text: Article about Ireland transformed is rousing stuff

indicators.note: something transformed has changed its form, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: AN is the indefinite article
taken as written

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece on a changed Ireland makes stirring reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper piece, but it is the grammatical article AN, mixed with all of IRELAND.
explanation.definitionFit: The hormone released in excitement or fear stirs up the body, which makes it literally stimulating stuff.

clue.text: Catch on handlebar perhaps causing pain

parts.note: to catch what someone says is to hear it
a handlebar is a kind of moustache, informally a tache; 'perhaps' marks the example

explanation.surface: Something snagging on a bicycle's handlebar gives the rider a painful moment.
explanation.walkthrough: The handlebar is not on a bike but on a face: a wide moustache with curled ends, shortened to TACHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartache is emotional anguish or sorrow, a kind of suffering.

clue.text: One choir remains in disarray whatever happens

indicators.note: disarray is disorder, so the letters are thrown out of their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Only a single choir is left, and it is in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: All fifteen letters of the first three words rearrange into the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means regardless of weather or circumstance, an assurance that something will go ahead.

clue.text: Where washing may be seen at every point?

definitions.text: Where washing may be seen at every point?

parts.note: surface reading: laundry pegged out on the washing line in the garden
setter's reading: an idiom meaning throughout, at every stage

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for 'at every stage' reads literally as the place clothes hang out to dry, strung the length of the washing line.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means at every stage or in every respect, and literally describes clothes hung throughout a washing line.

clue.text: Shylock's money, mostly owed, put with kitty

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: money owed is due
a kitty is a cat

explanation.surface: The moneylender's cash, largely owed to him, is added to the pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' suggests a pool of money in this financial scene, but it is a pet. Shylock is the moneylender in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Ducats were gold coins of Venice, the currency Shylock lends and demands back in the play.

clue.text: Wit from the south captivates one Nobel laureate

indicators.note: in a down entry, reading from the south means reading upwards, bottom to top
to captivate is to capture, so one piece holds another inside it

parts.note: a card is a witty, amusing person
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A southern comedian charms one prize-winner.
explanation.walkthrough: CARD takes in I to make CARID, then the whole is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Dirac, the British quantum physicist, shared the 1933 physics prize with Schrödinger.

clue.text: Mark sending Mike into unconscious state

indicators.note: sending something into a word places it inside that word

parts.note: a coma is a state of deep unconsciousness
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone called Mark knocks Mike out cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a man's name, but it is a punctuation mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A comma is a punctuation sign that separates parts of a sentence.

clue.text: Care to pay for the writer's entertainment and books

parts.note: to pay for someone's entertainment is to treat them, and the writer is ME, so 'treat me'
NT is the New Testament, the books of the Christian Bible's second part

explanation.surface: Would someone care to fund my night out, and buy me some books?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Care' reads as a verb, 'would you care to', but it is the noun. 'The writer' is the setter, giving ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Medical or nursing attention given to a patient is called their treatment.

clue.text: Mockery scars a wretched maiden

indicators.note: wretched means in a sorry state, so the letters are left in a mess

parts.note: taken as written
M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: Ridicule leaves a miserable young woman emotionally scarred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maiden' suggests a young woman, but in cricket a maiden is an over with no runs scored, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarcasm is cutting, ironic ridicule aimed at wounding or taunting someone.

clue.text: Society shunned by musketeer in liberal European city

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the pair of letters around it

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal
E is the abbreviation for European

indicators.note: what is shunned is kept away, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: Aramis is one of Dumas's Three Musketeers
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: A swordsman avoids polite company in a tolerant city on the Continent.
explanation.walkthrough: ARAMIS loses S and goes between L and E. 'European city' looks like the definition, but E is wordplay and the city is American.
explanation.definitionFit: Laramie is a city in Wyoming, home to the state's university.

clue.text: Bear — one sits regularly for surrealist

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter is taken

parts.note: the even-placed letters of these words

explanation.surface: A bear sits still at regular intervals to be painted by a surrealist.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the dash and take the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Ernst was a German painter central to the Dada and Surrealist movements.

clue.text: Far from keen, Frenchman volunteers to fill breach

indicators.note: to fill a gap is to go inside it, so these letters sit within another word

parts.note: a rent is a tear or split
Luc is a typical French man's name
the TA, Territorial Army, was Britain's volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: An unenthusiastic Frenchman steps up with the volunteers to plug a gap in the defences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breach' conjures a wall under siege, but it is simply a tear. The TA, Britain's former Territorial Army, is the usual crossword source for volunteers.
explanation.definitionFit: Reluctant means unwilling or hesitant, the very opposite of eager.

clue.text: Trace local banished from China for example

indicators.note: whatever is banished is sent away, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: China is an example of a republic
a local is one's neighbourhood pub

explanation.surface: Evidence of a native person being exiled from China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' is not a resident but the British word for one's nearest pub, removed from REPUBLIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A relic is a surviving remnant or vestige of something from the past.

clue.text: Sword beginning to tarnish beneath rising sea in French painting

indicators.note: in a down entry, what lies beneath comes after, lower in the column
in a down entry, something rising reads upwards, bottom to top

parts.note: mer is French for sea
brand is an old poetic word for a sword

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: A blade starting to tarnish sits under a rising sea in a French canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French painting' looks like a unit, but 'in French' belongs to the sea, and the painting is Dutch.
explanation.definitionFit: A canvas by the Dutch master Rembrandt van Rijn is itself called a Rembrandt, as an artwork named after its painter.

clue.text: Composition using organ in church — is it Bliss?

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so these letters are arranged afresh

parts.note: taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A church piece written for organ: could it be by the composer Arthur Bliss?
explanation.walkthrough: Bliss seems to be the English composer, but the clue plays on the saying 'ignorance is bliss'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'ignorance is bliss' equates not knowing with happiness, so the two nouns are treated as interchangeable.

clue.text: Unravelling sign lover's given out

indicators.note: something given out is scattered and distributed, so the letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lover's signal falls apart once it is broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolving a puzzle or mystery means untangling and working it out, just as unravelling one does.

clue.text: Mounted champion decapitated — it's terrifying!

indicators.note: to decapitate is to cut off the head, so the first letter goes

parts.note: a champion in armour is a knight, and mounted he sits on his mare: knight-mare

explanation.surface: A knight on horseback loses his head: a horrifying sight.
explanation.walkthrough: The knight and his mare run together, then the K goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightmare is a frightening dream or experience, so it is something that scares.

clue.text: Staff instruction to leave something on plate

parts.note: to staff a post is to man it
'get out!' orders someone to go

explanation.surface: Kitchen staff are told not to finish what's on their plates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave something on plate' reads as a table-manners instruction, but 'something on plate' is the definition. A mangetout is a snow pea, eaten pod and all.
explanation.definitionFit: Mangetout is a flat pea pod eaten whole, a vegetable served as part of a meal.

clue.text: Lot's regret voiced by Terah initially

parts.note: a sigh is regret expressed audibly

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: Biblical Lot's sorrow, expressed by his grandfather Terah at the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: Lot and Terah suggest Genesis, but 'Lot' is simply 'a lot', as in 'a sight better'.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal English 'a sight' means a great deal, as in 'a sight more than expected'.

clue.text: Relate what one remembers about car as cutting in

indicators.note: to cut a word is to cut it out, so those letters are removed

parts.note: re means about, concerning
the Mini is a classic British small car
as and since both mean because
taken as written

explanation.surface: Tell the story of a memorable car trip that involved someone pushing in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting in' sounds like a driver swerving into your lane; here IN is cut out of SINCE, leaving SCE.
explanation.definitionFit: To reminisce is to recall and talk about past experiences with pleasure.

clue.text: Somewhat wet politicians at centre in majority

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits inside it

parts.note: the majority is most

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter

parts.note: the sixth of eleven letters

explanation.surface: Wishy-washy centrist politicians form most of the chamber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet' suggests a feeble moderate politician, as in British Tory slang, but here it means damp.
explanation.definitionFit: Moist means slightly damp, a little wet rather than soaked through.

clue.text: Trap quickly springs up — end of mouse!

indicators.note: in a down entry, something springing up reads upwards, bottom to top

parts.note: soon means shortly, quickly

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: last letter

explanation.surface: A mousetrap snaps shut in an instant: curtains for the rodent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Springs' sounds like the trap's spring, but it signals the upward read.
explanation.definitionFit: A noose is a looped rope that tightens when pulled, used as a snare for animals.

clue.text: Flower to put back in boozer that's refused husband

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits inside it
what is refused is turned away, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: a lush is a heavy drinker
H is the abbreviation for husband

indicators.note: putting something back turns it round the other way

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone returns a flower to the pub, where a husband has been turned away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' is British slang for a pub, but here it is a drinker, LUSH, losing its H.
explanation.definitionFit: The lotus is an aquatic plant with large blooms, sacred in Hinduism and Buddhism.

clue.text: Flock seen aloft with grouse finally breaking cover

indicators.note: to break into something is to get inside it

parts.note: skin is an outer covering

indicators.note: finally points to the end of a word, its last letter

parts.note: last letter

explanation.surface: Birds fly overhead as a grouse flushes from its hiding place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like the bird in this game-shooting scene, but only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A skein is the collective term for wild geese in flight, strung out in a V.

clue.text: New look needing sash from Japan's capital

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
an air is a manner or appearance
an obi is the broad sash worn with a kimono

explanation.surface: A fresh outfit from Tokyo requires a kimono sash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Japan's capital' pretends to be Tokyo; the 's is 'is', and the capital is in Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Nairobi is the seat of government and largest city of Kenya.

clue.text: Do I lie with another having embraced sex appeal?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to embrace is to wrap arms around, so something ends up held inside

parts.note: to lie with another is to mate
it is old slang for sex appeal

explanation.surface: Should I sleep with someone else who is irresistibly attractive?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' opens like a question, but it is the definition, as in doing an impression of someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone, as a mimic does, is to copy or impersonate them.

clue.text: Tips to help all dodging fifty per cent in tax

indicators.note: each word dodges half of itself, so every one loses its second half

parts.note: first half
first half
first half

explanation.surface: Advice on helping everyone to avoid paying the higher rate of income tax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fifty per cent' suggests a tax rate; it means half of each of the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe is a levy of one tenth of produce or income, historically paid to the church.

clue.text: Ageless monarch good with soldiers in uniform

indicators.note: one group placed in another sits inside it

parts.note: even means uniform, regular
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
G is the abbreviation for good
the RE are the Royal Engineers

explanation.surface: A timeless queen and her good troops stand in their dress uniforms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' suggests military dress, but it is the adjective meaning level or regular, wrapped around the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Evergreen describes something perennially fresh or popular that never seems to go out of date.
